0.text: **Porphyrin synthesis** starts from glycine and succinyl-CoA: first **δ-aminolevulinic acid** (δ-ALA) is formed, then two molecules of δ-ALA give **porphobilinogen**, which has a pyrrole ring; four porphobilinogen molecules combine to give the porphyrin ring, and finally Fe^2+^ is inserted into it to form heme.

parts.text: **Porphyrias** are inherited deficiencies of the enzymes of heme synthesis. Intermediate products accumulate: in acute porphyria δ-ALA and porphobilinogen increase in the urine, causing severe abdominal pain and neurological disturbances (the urine darkens in light); in cutaneous porphyrias porphyrins accumulate in the skin and cause blisters on exposure to sunlight.

5.text: The four-membered **β-lactam ring** of β-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) is highly strained and reactive. It acylates the serine hydroxyl of the bacterial transpeptidase (penicillin-binding protein) and inactivates it irreversibly — cell wall synthesis stops. Many bacteria hydrolyze this ring with the enzyme **β-lactamase** and become resistant; **clavulanic acid** and **tazobactam** bind β-lactamase and protect the antibiotic.

parts.text: **Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and **tetracyclines** form insoluble chelates with Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^, Al^3+^ and Fe^2+^. If they are taken with milk, yogurt, antacids, iron or calcium preparations, their absorption falls several-fold. That is why these drugs are taken at least 2 hours apart from them.

insert.title: 0. Six-membered heterocycles containing oxygen and sulfur

blocks.text: **Pyran** is a six-membered ring with one oxygen atom. Its saturated form occurs in the **pyranose** form of monosaccharides (glucopyranose). **Benzopyran** (chromene) and **chromane**, fused with a benzene ring, form the basis of many plant substances and drugs.

parts.text: **Warfarin** is structurally similar to vitamin K; it blocks the enzyme that regenerates the active form of vitamin K (vitamin K epoxide reductase). As a result, less of the active forms of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X is formed in the liver. Treatment is monitored by the **INR**; if an overdose causes bleeding, **vitamin K** is given as the antidote.

blocks.text: **Alkaloids** are natural compounds, found mainly in plants, that contain a nitrogen heterocycle, have basic properties and exert strong physiological effects. In the plant they occur as salts with acids; in medicine their water-soluble salts are mostly used (atropine sulfate, morphine hydrochloride). Alkaloids are classified by the type of heterocycle.

blocks.text: **General precipitating reagents for alkaloids:** Dragendorff’s reagent (potassium bismuth iodide — orange precipitate), Mayer’s reagent (potassium mercuric iodide — white precipitate), tannin and picric acid. They form poorly soluble salts and complexes with the nitrogen atom of alkaloids — used to detect alkaloids in forensic toxicology.

parts.text: Many alkaloids have a narrow margin between therapeutic and toxic doses. **Tannin** (strongly brewed tea) forms insoluble compounds with them — that is why tannin solution was formerly used for gastric lavage in oral alkaloid poisoning.

skills.title: Skill: detecting alkaloids with general precipitating reagents

items: Pour 1 mL of the test solution (for example, a solution of an alkaloid salt) into each of 2–3 test tubes and acidify with 1–2 drops of dilute HCl.
Add 2 drops of Dragendorff’s reagent to the first tube — an orange or reddish precipitate indicates an alkaloid.
Add Mayer’s reagent to the second tube — a white or yellowish precipitate is observed.
Add tannin solution to the third tube — a whitish-yellow precipitate forms.
As a control, perform the same reactions with distilled water and compare the results; confirm a positive result with specific reactions to identify the particular alkaloid.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: Two children ate jimsonweed seeds in a field. Their skin is red and dry, the pupils are dilated and do not react to light, there is tachycardia, the temperature is raised, and the children are agitated and delirious.
cases.ask: Poisoning with which substances? To which group of alkaloids do they belong and how do they act?
cases.answer: Jimsonweed contains **tropane alkaloids** — **atropine** and scopolamine. They are competitive antagonists of acetylcholine at M-cholinergic receptors: secretion of the salivary and sweat glands stops (dry skin, hyperthermia), the pupils dilate, the heart rate increases, and there is CNS excitation and delirium. Help: gastric lavage, activated charcoal (binds alkaloids well), cooling; in severe cases the cholinesterase inhibitor **physostigmine** increases acetylcholine and overcomes the blockade.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve takes warfarin (the INR should be 2.5–3.5). After he began to eat large amounts of spinach and cabbage, the INR fell to 1.6.
cases.ask: Why did the INR fall? Explain the relationship between warfarin and vitamin K.
cases.answer: Warfarin is a coumarin derivative; it blocks **vitamin K epoxide reductase**, which reactivates vitamin K, and reduces the formation of active clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Spinach and cabbage contain a lot of **vitamin K**: the increased dietary vitamin K partly overcomes the effect of warfarin, more clotting factors are formed and the INR falls — the risk of thrombosis increases. The patient is advised to eat vitamin K-rich foods in a steady amount without sharp changes.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with a urinary tract infection took ciprofloxacin tablets every day with a glass of milk and, for heartburn, together with an antacid. After three days the fever and symptoms persist.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical reason for the failure of treatment. What would you advise?
cases.answer: The **keto and carboxyl groups** in the fluoroquinolone molecule form a stable, insoluble **chelate** with Ca^2+^ (milk), Mg^2+^ and Al^3+^ (antacid) ions. The chelate is not absorbed in the intestine — the antibiotic concentration in blood and urine does not reach an effective level. Advice: take ciprofloxacin with water, and take dairy products, antacids, iron and calcium preparations at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after the drug.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A child’s otitis was treated with amoxicillin without effect. Culture showed a β-lactamase-producing Haemophilus. The doctor switched to amoxicillin + clavulanic acid.
cases.ask: Why did amoxicillin not work? How does clavulanic acid help?
cases.answer: The active part of amoxicillin is the strained **β-lactam ring**: it acylates transpeptidase and stops cell wall synthesis. The bacterial enzyme **β-lactamase** hydrolyzes and opens this ring — the antibiotic becomes inactive. **Clavulanic acid** also has a β-lactam structure: it binds β-lactamase irreversibly and inactivates it (a “suicide” inhibitor), so amoxicillin is preserved and acts.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A young man found unconscious has slow, shallow breathing (6 breaths per minute), pinpoint pupils and injection marks on his arm.
cases.ask: Poisoning with substances of which alkaloid group is suspected? How does the antidote act?
cases.answer: The clinical triad — coma, respiratory depression, **miosis** — is typical of poisoning with **opioids** (morphine, heroin — morphinan derivatives with an isoquinoline skeleton). They stimulate μ-opioid receptors in the brain and depress the respiratory center. The antidote is **naloxone**: its structure is close to that of morphine, but it does not activate the receptor; as a **competitive antagonist** it displaces the opioid from the receptor, and breathing recovers within minutes. Naloxone acts briefly, so the patient is kept under observation and the dose is repeated if necessary.
